```text
 | |                      SQL text                        |       |         |
 | +------------------------------------------------------+       |         |
 |      |                                                         |         |
 |      v                                                         |         |
 | Standard database API                                          |         |
 |   DB-API 2.0 (Python)  /  DBI (R)                              |         |
 |      |                                                         |         |
 |      v                                                         |         |
 | Driver / adapter                                               |         |
 |   psycopg (Python)  /  RPostgres (R)                           |         |
 |   rows come back as tuples / data frames (collect()),          |         |
 |   or as the ORM's objects (county.name)                        |         |
 |      |                                                         |         |
 |      v                                                         v         |
 | libpq: Postgres's own C client library, used by all of the above         |
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                          |      ^
                 SQL text |      | rows back
                          v      |
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 | CONNECTION, speaking the Postgres wire protocol over                     |
 |   a Unix socket (/var/run/postgresql on your laptop)                     |
 |   or TCP on a remote machine (host:5432). (Not covered in this class).   |
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                          |      ^
                          v      |
 SERVER SIDE: the database
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
 | Postgres server (postmaster)                                             |
 |   listens, checks who you are, starts one backend per connection         |
 |      |                                                                   |
 |      v                                                                   |
 | Backend process (one per connection)                                     |
 |   parser  ->  planner (what EXPLAIN shows)  ->  executor                 |
 |      |      ^                                                            |
 |      v      |                                                            |
 | Data directory (PGDATA) on disk                                          |
 |   tables and indexes, stored as 8 kB pages                               |
 +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The convenience of all three has a price: when a query is slow you have to read the SQL they generated (`show_query` in `dbplyr`, `ibis.to_sql` in `ibis`, the query log in an ORM) to see why, so you still need to know SQL. ORMs in particular make it easy to write a loop such as "for each county, print `county.state.name`", which quietly sends one query per county which is extremely inefficient. I have so many of my own stories about this!

## Conclusion of Postgres and the SQL unit as itself

How large is the postgres software package (not including any databases)? Add it up, with `du` ("disk usage") for the program files and the database itself for your data:

```bash
du -ch /usr/lib/postgresql /usr/share/postgresql | tail -n 1   # for linus users
du -shL "$(brew --prefix postgresql@18)" #for macos users
```

That is a lot of space for a program whose job is to store rows in a table. But look at what it bought you in this unit:

- **Speed:** the same question went from scanning every row (about 70 ms here, and growing with the table) to under 1 ms with an index, and that stays true as the table grows.
- **Correctness:** typed columns refused `'N/A'` as a number, and rules such as `NOT NULL` and `UNIQUE` can refuse other nonsense when it arrives.
- **Safe changes:** single-row updates and transactions that happen completely or not at all, even if the machine crashes.
- **Many users at once:** many programs reading and writing the same tables at once without corrupting them.
- **A query language** instead of one-off shell pipelines: SQL, with joins, grouping and sorting, and a planner that picks how to run each query.

PostgreSQL grew out of research at Berkeley in the 1980s and has had decades of engineering since. Nobody would write all of that again for one analysis. It's another "truly amazing" piece of software, a pinnacle of human achievement.

But not every job needs a heavyweight server running on linux. When one analyst queries data that mostly gets read, not written, a lightweight database is often enough, and for analytics the most popular is **DuckDB**. It has no server: it is a program you run from the shell, much as you run `psql`, or a library you load inside Python or R through its own driver (in R, only the `dbConnect(...)` line changes). A whole database is one file, or no file at all. It speaks almost the same SQL as Postgres, so the queries of this unit, window functions included, mostly run unchanged, and it can query a CSV or Parquet file directly, without loading it first. Its storage is columnar (Lecture 6), which makes it very fast for aggregates over a few columns of many rows. What it gives up is the "many users at once" point above: it is not built for many programs writing to the same tables. Since it is close to a drop-in replacement for the more universal, full-featured, robust Postgres you now know, we will not cover it separately.

## Why clean in SQL and not in R or Python?

Every step of this pipeline can also be done in R or Python, once the data has been pulled in through a database driver. `dplyr` or `data.table` in R and `pandas` in Python have a ready-made function for each of them: dropping exact duplicates, keeping the newest row per key, computing flags with a lag, and turning sentinels into missing values. Still, SQL is often preferred for the rule-based steps, for these reasons:

* **Always current.** A view is recomputed on every query, so tomorrow's feed is cleaned the moment it arrives. A script has to be rerun, and the cleaned file it wrote goes stale in between.
* **The data does not have to fit in memory.** `pandas`, `dplyr` and `data.table` hold the whole table in RAM, and it first has to travel over the network to get there. The database works on disk with its indexes, next to the data, and sends back only the answer, as in "Let the database do the work" above. For big data, this is often what decides it.
* **Language-neutral.** One team member uses R, another Python, a third a BI tool (like Tableau/PowerBI). SQL is the one language all of them can read and query.
* **One copy of the rules.** Cleaning scripts in R, Python, BI tools get copied from project to project and drift apart, until two analysts report two different numbers from the same raw table.
* **Dashboards read from the database.** BI tools such as Tableau and Power BI connect straight to the database and are usually pointed at a view, so they show the cleaned data without any extra work. Both also have their own cleaning tools (Tableau Prep, Power BI's Power Query), but rules written there usually live inside that tool (a Prep flow, a Power BI report), where no R or Python user can see or reuse them. Cleaning in a view keeps the dashboard and the analysis consistent.
* **Auditable.** The raw table is never touched, and every rule is a short, readable line in a view. Tools like dbt (which we won't cover) add version control and tests on top.

R and Python are the better choice for what SQL does badly: model-based imputation (`mice`, `missForest`), fuzzy matching with dedicated libraries, heavy text parsing, and exploratory plots to find the problems in the first place. The usual pattern combines the two. SQL views do low-level rule-based cleaning like we saw above, and R or Python pulls the last view through a driver for modeling.

## Big picture plan

We will be using database adapters as we "put it all together": from databases -> cleaning -> predictive modeling / inferential modeling using R and/or Python. That's when we'll dip into knowledge from all your other statistics and machine learning courses.

# Data Frames in R and Python

::: {.callout-note}
## Not covered on the exam
This unit is FYI reading only: it will not be tested.
:::

A driver hands the result of a query to R or Python as a **data frame**, and from then on the work happens in memory, in whichever data-frame library you chose. There are several, and they differ more than their similar names suggest: in syntax, in speed, and in whether they use one core or all of them. This unit compares five of them on `covid`. Nothing in it is new statistics; it is a buyer's guide.

## The libraries

| Library               | Language | In one line                                                                              |
|:----------------------|:---------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `data.frame` (base R) | R        | built in, no packages needed; the baseline, and slow on big data                         |
| `dplyr` (tidyverse)   | R        | readable verbs joined by pipes; `dbplyr` turns the same verbs into SQL (above)           |
| `data.table`          | R        | the fastest in R, with a terse `dt[i, j, by]` syntax, and changes data in place          |
| `pandas`              | Python   | the standard in Python, with a row index; most operations use one core                   |
| `polars`              | Python   | newer, columnar (Arrow), uses all cores, and can plan a whole query first (lazy mode)    |

: Five data-frame libraries. `polars` also exists for R, and `data.table` has a Python port, but both are mostly used in the language shown.

## The same two questions in each library

Two questions from this lecture, asked five times: the three states with the most cases on 2020-12-31 (the query from the drivers section), and the daily new cases per county with `lag`, counting the days that went negative (the `cases_went_down` flag of the cleaning view). Every version gives California 2307860, Texas 1770527, Florida 1323307 and 15144.

Base R needs no packages. `aggregate` groups, and `ave` applies a function within each group, here "shift down by one":

```{r}
setwd("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03")     # where covid.csv lives
covid <- read.csv("covid.csv", colClasses = c(fips = "character"))
covid$date <- as.Date(covid$date)
dec31 <- covid[covid$date == as.Date("2020-12-31"), ]
top <- aggregate(cases ~ state, data = dec31, FUN = sum)
head(top[order(-top$cases), ], 3)                           # California 2307860, Texas 1770527, Florida 1323307
covid <- covid[order(covid$state, covid$county, covid$date), ]
covid$new_cases <- covid$cases - ave(covid$cases, covid$state, covid$county, FUN = function(v) c(0, head(v, -1)))
sum(covid$new_cases < 0)                                    # 15144
```

`dplyr` reads like the SQL, one verb per clause, in the order the steps happen. `lag(cases, 1, default = 0)` is the same as SQL's `lag(cases, 1, 0)`:

```{r}
setwd("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03")
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
covid <- read_csv("covid.csv", col_types = cols(fips = col_character()))
covid |>
  filter(date == as.Date("2020-12-31")) |>                 # WHERE
  group_by(state) |>                                        # GROUP BY
  summarise(cases = sum(cases)) |>                          # SELECT sum(cases)
  arrange(desc(cases)) |>                                   # ORDER BY ... DESC
  head(3)                                                   # LIMIT 3
covid <- covid |>
  arrange(state, county, date) |>
  group_by(state, county) |>                                # PARTITION BY
  mutate(new_cases = cases - lag(cases, 1, default = 0)) |> # a window function: every row is kept
  ungroup()
sum(covid$new_cases < 0)                                    # 15144
```

`data.table` puts everything inside the brackets: `dt[i, j, by]` reads "take rows `i`, compute `j`, grouped by `by`". `:=` adds the column *in place*, without copying the table, which is a large part of its speed and memory advantage:

```{r}
setwd("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03")
library(data.table)
covid <- fread("covid.csv", colClasses = c(fips = "character"))
covid[date == as.IDate("2020-12-31"), .(cases = sum(cases)), by = state][order(-cases)][1:3]
setorder(covid, state, county, date)                       # sorts in place, too
covid[, new_cases := cases - shift(cases, 1, fill = 0), by = .(state, county)]
covid[new_cases < 0, .N]                                    # 15144
```

`pandas` chains methods. `groupby(...)["cases"].shift()` is its `lag`:

```{python}
import os
os.chdir(os.path.expanduser("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03"))
import pandas as pd
covid = pd.read_csv("covid.csv", dtype={"fips": "string"}, parse_dates=["date"])
(covid[covid["date"] == "2020-12-31"]
   .groupby("state", as_index=False)["cases"].sum()
   .sort_values("cases", ascending=False)
   .head(3))                                                # California 2307860, Texas 1770527, Florida 1323307
covid = covid.sort_values(["state", "county", "date"])
covid["new_cases"] = covid["cases"] - covid.groupby(["state", "county"])["cases"].shift(1, fill_value=0)
(covid["new_cases"] < 0).sum()                              # 15144
```

`polars` looks like `pandas` at first glance but is a different design. You write **expressions** (`pl.col("cases").sum()`) instead of indexing, there is no row index, and `.over(...)` is SQL's `OVER (PARTITION BY ...)`. Code written for `pandas` must be rewritten, not just re-imported:

```{python}
import os
os.chdir(os.path.expanduser("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec03"))
import polars as pl
covid = pl.read_csv("covid.csv", schema_overrides={"fips": pl.Utf8}, try_parse_dates=True)
(covid.filter(pl.col("date") == pl.date(2020, 12, 31))
      .group_by("state").agg(pl.col("cases").sum())
      .sort("cases", descending=True)
      .head(3))                                             # California 2307860, Texas 1770527, Florida 1323307
covid = covid.sort(["state", "county", "date"]).with_columns(
    new_cases = pl.col("cases") - pl.col("cases").shift(1, fill_value=0).over(["state", "county"]))
covid.filter(pl.col("new_cases") < 0).height                # 15144
```

`polars` also has a **lazy** mode: `scan_csv` instead of `read_csv` builds a plan and runs nothing until `collect()`. Like Postgres's planner, it then rearranges the work. `explain()` shows that the filter and the column choice were pushed into the scan itself, so only 3 of the 6 columns are ever read, and only the December 31 rows are kept:

```{python}
lazy = (pl.scan_csv("covid.csv", schema_overrides={"fips": pl.Utf8}, try_parse_dates=True)
          .filter(pl.col("date") == pl.date(2020, 12, 31))
          .group_by("state").agg(pl.col("cases").sum())
          .sort("cases", descending=True)
          .head(3))
print(lazy.explain())                                       # Csv SCAN [covid.csv]  PROJECT 3/6 COLUMNS  SELECTION: col("date") == 2020-12-31
lazy.collect()                                              # the same three states
```

## How fast are they?

Six everyday operations, timed in seconds on `covid.csv` (884,737 rows, 36 MB), the median of 5 runs, with the fastest in each row in bold:

| operation                                  | base R | `dplyr` | `data.table` | `pandas` |  `polars` |
|:-------------------------------------------|-------:|--------:|-------------:|---------:|----------:|
| read the CSV                               |   3.48 |    0.56 |         0.15 |     0.83 | **0.036** |
| filter: Texas rows                         |  0.009 |   0.010 |    **0.005** |    0.008 |     0.010 |
| group by state and day, sum                |   0.90 |   0.083 |    **0.021** |    0.042 |     0.021 |
| window: new cases per county               |   2.51 |    0.29 |     **0.11** |     0.19 |      0.16 |
| join: each row with its county's first day |   5.95 |    0.12 |        0.062 |     0.16 | **0.049** |
| sort by cases                              |  0.090 |   0.085 |        0.096 |     0.19 | **0.055** |

: `covid.csv`, 884,737 rows. Seconds, median of 5 runs.

At this size, every library except base R answers everything in under a second, so pick by syntax, not speed. The differences appear at scale. The same operations on `covid_big.csv` from Lecture 3 (50 copies of `covid`: 44,236,850 rows, 1.8 GB), one run each:

| operation                                  | base R | `dplyr` | `data.table` | `pandas` | `polars` |
|:-------------------------------------------|-------:|--------:|-------------:|---------:|---------:|
| read the CSV                               |  238.2 |    25.5 |          8.0 |     46.6 |  **2.4** |
| filter: Texas rows                         |   10.2 |    0.59 |         0.41 |     0.45 | **0.27** |
| group by state and day, sum                |  205.8 |     2.5 |     **0.68** |      3.0 |      4.3 |
| window: new cases per county               |  572.8 |    13.4 |      **5.6** |     31.0 |     24.5 |
| join: each row with its county's first day |  801.4 |     7.7 |          6.8 |     10.3 |  **2.4** |
| sort by cases                              |    8.8 |    11.9 |      **8.5** |     31.3 |      8.6 |

: `covid_big.csv`, 44 million rows. Seconds, one run.

What the numbers say:

* **Base R does not scale.** The join took over 13 minutes and the window almost 10, against seconds for everything else. Its `aggregate`, `ave` and `merge` were not built for tens of millions of rows. Use it for small data and for teaching, not for big data.
* **`data.table` and `polars` lead**, and they trade first places. `polars` is fastest at reading (all cores parse the file at once) and at the join; `data.table` at grouping and the window. Both are often several times faster than `dplyr` and `pandas`, but not on every operation: here `polars` grouped more slowly than `pandas`.
* **`dplyr` and `pandas` are fine up to a few million rows**, and they have the most users, documentation and answers online. That is often worth more than a few seconds.
* **Memory matters as much as time.** The Python run peaked at 16.5 GB of RAM for a 1.8 GB CSV: the table itself takes more room in memory than in the file, and many operations (the sorts, the window) make a full copy of it. `data.table`'s in-place `:=` and `polars`'s lazy mode avoid many of those copies. When the data does not fit in RAM at all, none of these work, and the database (or Parquet with `arrow` or `polars`'s lazy scans) is the answer, as the "data does not have to fit in memory" point above says.

Benchmarks are a snapshot, not a ranking for all time. These were run on one 12-thread laptop (WSL2, 41 GB of RAM) with Python 3.14, `pandas` 3.0.6 and `polars` 1.44.2, and R (development version of October 2026) with `dplyr` 1.2.1, `readr` 2.2.0 and `data.table` 1.18.4, which used 6 threads by default while `polars` used all 12. A different machine, a different version or a different operation can reorder the middle of the table. Time your own job before you switch libraries for speed.

## Which one when?

* **Already in R, data in the millions of rows:** `dplyr` for readability. Switch to `data.table` (or `dtplyr`, which runs `dplyr` code on `data.table`) when it gets slow.
* **Already in Python:** `pandas` is what every tutorial and most libraries expect (`scikit-learn`, `statsmodels`, plotting). Reach for `polars` when the data is large, and convert with `.to_pandas()` at the end if a library needs it.
* **Bigger than memory, or shared:** keep it in the database and pull only the answer (the "Let the database do the work" section above), or keep it in Parquet and scan it lazily.
